Section 208(b)(3) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3), requires that immigration judges consider "all relevant factors" when evaluating an asylum claim, including "the applicant's employment history and any other relevant evidence" (see also, Rodriguez v. Garland, 942 F.3d 897, 903 (9th Cir. 2020)).

Additionally, the Ninth Circuit's decision in Kasinga v. INS, 287 F.3d 1091 (9th Cir. 2002), establishes a clear precedent for the use of occupational records as corroborating evidence in asylum claims. In Kasinga, the court held that "an applicant's documentation of employment in a targeted profession can be sufficient to establish a well-founded fear of persecution" (Kasinga, 287 F.3d at 1097). This holding is directly applicable to the present case, where the asylum applicant's documented employment history within a hospital system known to be targeted by state actors constitutes corroborating evidence of a well-founded fear of persecution.
